sources.citation: Naitoro, Katerina. 2019. Morphs in search of meaning: Southeast Solomonic transitive morphology in diachronic perspective. PhD thesis, School of Culture, History and Language, The Australian National University. doi:10.25911/5d51485137845; hdl:1885/163714.
sources.note: No phonology section for any language; Birao appears in ~130 places as morphological data (causative vagha-, transitive -Ci-, hini- preposition; 'in my field data from Birao there are 333 verbs with transitive forms'). The only prosodic remarks are family-level and second-hand: p.220 'The descriptions available for SES languages rarely discuss specifics of stress assignment in verbs with longer suffixes'; p.350 'As pointed out by Ross (pers.com. 14.7.2018), these languages all have CV syllable structure and unstressed vowels lose little or no quality'. Birao forms are cited without stress mar…

sources.citation: Greenhill, Simon J., Robert Blust & Russell D. Gray (eds.). 2008-. Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database, language no. 548 'Mbirao' (ISO brr; source: Tryon & Hackman 1983; data entry Michael Dunn; 215 items). Leipzig: MPI-EVA (abvd.eva.mpg.de); also Lexibank abvd CLDF ID 548.

sources.note: Nothing. Notes field contains only the Tryon & Hackman citation; the 215 forms (e.g. 'lima-na' hand, 'tua-na' leg, 'lela' walk, 'sala' road, 'mate' die, 'vatu' stone) are in T&H's orthography with no stress or length marks; no prosodic remark anywhere on the page (the only 'tone' string is in 'stone').

sources.citation: Lynch, John, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley. 2002. The Oceanic Languages. Richmond: Curzon. p.110, p.884.
sources.note: Birao named only in the Southeast Solomonic subgrouping (West Guadalcanal-Talise-Malango-Birao) and the language listing with no source; nothing on its phonology.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm D. 1988. Proto Oceanic and the Austronesian languages of Western Melanesia. Pacific Linguistics C-98. Canberra: ANU. (Same work as container 7; additional target coverage: ch. 3 reflex sets pp. 41-92 and Appendix B.6 'South-East Solomonic' p. 410 cite Bauro, Birao, Malango, Dori'o and Kwai from Tryon & Hackman 1983.)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201.R67 1988)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201 .R67 1988
sources.note: Cited only as a source of lexical reflexes in the Proto-Oceanic consonant chapter (ch. 3) and listed in Appendix B.6 with 'Tryon and Hackman (1983) served as a lexical source for all the languages listed below'; no synchronic phonology or prosody of any South-East Solomonic language is given, and the word 'stress' occurs in the book only on p. 7 (notation) and pp. 86-87 (Ali, North New Guinea cluster).

sources.citation: Crowley, Susan Smith. 1986. Tolo Dictionary. Pacific Linguistics C-91. Canberra: ANU. Introduction, 'Stress' (Rosetta Project excerpt rosettaproject_tlr_ortho-2). [SISTER LANGUAGE Tolo/Talise tali1259, not Birao]
sources.note: For Tolo only: 'In Tolo the stress is nearly always placed on the next to last syllable regardless of the number of syllables in the word', with pronouns hamitou/hamutou initial-stressed and a marked final-stress class. Says nothing about Birao.

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. & B. D. Hackman. 1983. Solomon Islands Languages: An Internal Classification. Pacific Linguistics C-72. Canberra: ANU. (Mbirao = list no. 56)
sources.note: Nothing. Mbirao appears only as a 324-item wordlist (no stress marks) and in sound-correspondence tables; a full-text search for stress/accent/penultimate finds no prosodic statement for any Guadalcanal language.

sources.citation: Simons, Gary F. 1982. Word taboo and comparative Austronesian linguistics. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 3: Accent on variety, 157-226. Pacific Linguistics C-76. Canberra: Australian National University. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/253300; Birao = sample language no. 50)
sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or tone for Birao or any other language: the paper is about name and word taboo as a driver of lexical replacement. The Birao entry lists five taboo practices (no naming of relatives-by-marriage; brother/sister and MB/ZS name avoidance; the common word homophonous with a tabooed name is itself tabooed; a speaker addressing a tabooed relative uses the dual pronoun). a full-text search for stress/accent over the whole 3,341-line text for stress|accent|penult|tone|intonat returns only the volume title 'Accent on variety'.

sources.citation: Tryon, D. T. 1982. Towards a classification of Solomon Islands languages. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 97-108. Pacific Linguistics C-74. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Classification only; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Hackman, Brian D. 1971. List of Solomon Islands Vernaculars (ordered according to number of speakers; 1970 census; indication of published literature). n.p. [Honiara]. Reprinted in: Huebner, Thom (comp.) 1979. Solomon Islands Pijin: Special Skills Handbook (Peace Corps Language Handbook Series). Brattleboro, VT: The Experiment in International Living / School for International Training, section 'Solomon Islands Vernaculars Learning Guide'. ERIC microfiche; archive.org item micro_IA41153606_0095.
sources.note: No phonology content. The complete Mbirao entry reads: 'Mbirao (MN) East Central Guadalcanal. 3,209, but serves over 4,000 if Tolo and Talise included. Orthography available, some study by RCM.' - i.e. a POINTER to an unpublished Roman Catholic (Marist) Mission orthography/study of Mbirao existing before 1971.
